target.title: fix(ui): keep agent avatar initials on grapheme clusters
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Control UI agent avatar fallbacks used `.slice(0, 1)` on the agent name/id.
Names starting with a flag emoji (`🇺🇸Team`) or ZWJ sequence (`👨‍💻Dev`) were
cut mid-cluster and rendered as replacement characters / incomplete glyphs.
Engines without `Intl.Segmenter` also dropped safe non-ASCII BMP letters
(e.g. `東京`, `Émile`) to `?` when only ASCII `[A-Za-z0-9]` was accepted.

## Why This Change Was Made

Add `resolveFallbackAvatarInitial` using `Intl.Segmenter` grapheme granularity
and use it in the three agent avatar fallback call sites. Keep the prior
locale-independent `toUpperCase()` casing contract (not `toLocaleUpperCase()`).

When `Intl.Segmenter` is unavailable, take the first **code point** only when it
is a single BMP Unicode letter (`\p{L}`) or decimal digit (`\p{Nd}`). Do **not**
use UTF-16 `.slice` or non-BMP first-code-point emoji (flags / ZWJ) — those stay
`?` so incomplete glyphs are never shown.

## User Impact

**Before:** Agent names beginning with multi-code-point emoji produced broken
avatar initials; non-ASCII letter names became `?` without Segmenter.

**After:** Fallback avatars keep a complete grapheme (flag / ZWJ emoji / letter)
with Segmenter. Without Segmenter, safe BMP letters/digits still render
(`東京` → `東`, `Émile` → `É`) while flag/ZWJ-leading names show `?`.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetches the official installer and pipes it straight into bash. Current `origin/main` bounds that pipe with `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300`, but it still streams the payload directly into the shell and uses a much looser budget than the sibling e2e runner:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh (current origin/main)
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 -- "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

This PR brings the non-root runner to the same **download-then-execute** contract as the sibling e2e runner merged in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`): download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, verify curl completed, then execute it, then clean up.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fail fast on stall:** `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged for the sibling installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911). A stalled fetch fails the step in under 2 minutes instead of tying up the runner for 5.
- **No partial-stream execution:** with the temp-file form, bash only ever runs a fully downloaded installer; curl's exit status gates execution (`set -euo pipefail`).
- **Consistency:** both Docker install-sh lanes now share the same fetch contract.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download fails fast with a clear curl error instead of streaming into a long-hanging pipe. Identical install semantics on success.

## Evidence

After (this PR, `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh`):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
# Download the installer to a temp file first so a stalled connection or hung
# response body cannot wedge the container run forever. Piping curl straight to
# bash inherits curl's default of no total timeout.
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Regression tests (final head `15ad709b`, rebased onto latest main):

```bash
pnpm vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  77 passed (77)
```

Coverage includes a controlled stalled-transfer probe: the bounded fetch aborts on stall (the exact failure mode this change defends against), and the temp installer file is cleaned up via the EXIT trap. The runner-assertion test now checks the bounded temp-file form (`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer"` + `bash "$installer"`).

## Real Docker smoke (current head `d1a1adef6e0`, rebased onto latest main)

Full non-root Docker smoke against the real installer endpoint (`https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`), colima/arm64, image built from `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/Dockerfile` (which COPYs this head's `run.sh`), exact harness env (`OPENCLAW_NO_ONBOARD=1`, `OPENCLAW_NO_PROMPT=1`, `OPENCLAW_INSTALL_METHOD=npm`):

```text

==> Pre-flight: ensure supported Node is already present
==> Run installer (non-root user)          # download-to-file + bash "$installer" path under test
✓ Git installed
✓ npm configured for user installs
✓ OpenClaw npm package installed
✓ OpenClaw installed
🦞 OpenClaw installed successfully (2026.7.1-2)!
==> Verify git installed
==> Verify CLI installed
cli=openclaw installed=2026.7.1-2 expected=2026.7.1-2
==> Sanity: CLI runs
OK
```

The download-then-execute success path works end-to-end in the real non-root container: the bounded curl fetch completes to a temp file, `bash "$installer"` runs it, git and the CLI verify, and the runner exits `OK`.

## What was not tested

Nothing material: the success path is proven by the real Docker run above, the stall path by the hermetic stalled-transfer probe in the suite.

## CI note

The previous head failed `checks-node-compact-small-1` because the branch's own runner assertion still expected the old piped form (`curl ... | bash`) that this PR replaces. The assertion is aligned with the temp-file fetch on the current head, and the branch is rebased onto latest main.

target.title: fix(acp): background Codex ACP turns fail hard on transient pre-output Internal error
target.body:
Related: #85207

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where background Codex ACP child turns fail hard with a bare `AcpRuntimeError: Internal error` (`code=ACP_TURN_FAILED`) before the agent has produced any output. Parent workflows that spawn ACP child sessions see a terminal blocker with no deliverable, even though the failure happened before any prompt side effects and a single retry would have succeeded.

Issue #85207 contains two asks: a bounded pre-side-effect retry (labeled `clawsweeper:fix-shape-clear`) and a stale ACPX install policy (labeled `clawsweeper:needs-product-decision`). This PR implements only the retry leaf. The stale-install policy remains a maintainer product decision and is not touched.

## Why This Change Was Made

The manager turn runner already owns the right machinery: a two-attempt loop, a `sawTurnOutput` side-effect guard, and a one-time fresh-handle retry used today for early acpx exits and structured `SESSION_RESUME_REQUIRED` failures (`src/acp/control-plane/manager.runtime-resume-state.ts`). The transient failure shapes reported in the issue were simply not eligible, so they surfaced immediately.

This change extends `prepareFreshManagerRuntimeHandleRetry` with a transient-shape predicate: a trimmed message equal to `Internal error` (the generic ACP JSON-RPC internal error the Codex ACP path emits when no diagnostics are available), or a client/connection/query closed transport shape (`codex app-server client is closed` from `extensions/codex/src/app-server/client.ts`, `query closed before response received` from the acpx transport). Eligibility still requires `attempt === 0` and no observed turn output, so there is exactly one retry and never a retry after assistant output or tool calls.

Design boundaries:

- Structured `SESSION_RESUME_REQUIRED` recovery keeps priority; the transient retry only clears the in-memory runtime handle and never discards the persistent session identity, preserving the #87830 boundary (no `prepareFreshSession`, resume id kept).
- Matching is top-level message only, deliberately not the cause chain: the acpx Codex stderr enrichment wraps the bare generic error as `cause`, so a cause-chain walk would make every enriched deterministic failure (for example an auth error in the stderr tail) retryable. Enriched messages retry only when the enriched text itself carries a closed-transport shape.
- The retry lives at the manager boundary, which already owns retry policy and the side-effect guard. Retrying inside the acpx runtime `startTurn` would require buffering event streams and cannot see manager-level output state; the sibling `runTurn`/`startTurn` enrichment paths in `extensions/acpx/src/runtime.ts` are unchanged and both feed this same manager catch path.

Prior art: #59883 attempted a broader multi-retry backoff at the `runTurn` layer and was closed after its head drifted to unrelated work. This PR is a single bounded retry using the manager infrastructure that landed since.

## User Impact

Background ACP/Codex child work now survives one transient pre-output prompt failure (generic internal error or closed transport) instead of failing the whole parent task. Sessions keep their persistent identity across the retry. Behavior after any observed output is unchanged, a second failure surfaces exactly as before, and non-transient failures (including enriched diagnostics such as auth errors) are never retried.

## Evidence

Live before/after driving the real `AcpSessionManager` (`getAcpSessionManager().initializeSession` + `runTurn`, the same production dispatcher the gateway uses), with the real turn runner, retry policy, and SQLite session store in an isolated state dir. Only the ACP child agent process boundary is scripted, registered through the production `registerAcpRuntimeBackend` API, to fail the first prompt with the issue's exact error and stream output on the second. Identical inputs both runs.

BEFORE (pristine main d0f37bd8433782147629bdd2fc1b076c1def61d3):

```
turn outcome: failed code=ACP_TURN_FAILED message=Internal error
prompt attempts that reached the codex acp agent: 1
events seen by the parent workflow: error:Internal error
```

AFTER (this patch, identical inputs):

```
acp-manager: retrying agent:codex:acp:issue-85207-repro with a fresh runtime handle after transient pre-output turn failure: Internal error
acp-manager: session identity updated for agent:codex:acp:issue-85207-repro (agentSessionId <none> -> <none>, acpxSessionId acpx-sid-85207 -> acpx-sid-85207, acpxRecordId <none> -> <none>)
turn outcome: completed
prompt attempts that reached the codex acp agent: 2
events seen by the parent workflow: error:Internal error | text_delta:child task result | done
```

The parent-visible outcome flips from a hard `ACP_TURN_FAILED` blocker to a completed turn with the child deliverable, and the session identity line shows the persistent id preserved across the retry.

Regression coverage in `src/acp/control-plane/manager.turn-results.test.ts` (5 of the new cases fail on pristine main, all 24 pass with the patch): retry for bare internal error, closed app-server client, and closed query shapes with the resume id preserved and `prepareFreshSession` never called; retry for a thrown transient failure; no retry after output was seen; no second retry; no retry for enriched non-transient diagnostics.

Local gates (changed files): `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/acp/control-plane/manager.turn-results.test.ts` 24 passed; `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` clean; `oxfmt --check` clean; `tsgo` core and core-test lanes exit 0.

Not tested live: a real Codex app-server crash mid-prompt; the transient failure is injected at the registered runtime backend boundary.

target.title: fix(context-engine): bound deferred turn maintenance with a per-task timeout (AI-assisted)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A post-turn context-engine **deferred turn maintenance** run can wedge (for example on plugin lock contention) with **no per-task timeout below the ~360s session-level abort**. While it is wedged it holds its maintenance lane, so a user message queued behind it on the same session can wait minutes before being processed, even though the model is healthy. `session.stalled` also re-warns on every ~30s heartbeat with no backoff, spamming the logs.

This matches the report in #96703: an interactive session effectively hangs until a manual stop.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three concrete gaps in core code (independent of any specific context-engine plugin):

1. **No per-task timeout was available on the maintenance enqueue.** `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance` enqueued the maintenance worker via `enqueueCommandInLane(...)` with no options. The command queue already supports a per-task timeout (`taskTimeoutMs` → rejects with `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` and releases the lane), but the maintenance lane never wired it up, so an operator hitting the wedge had no knob below the session-level abort.
2. **A timed-out maintenance worker was not fenced.** Rejecting the enqueue promise releases the lane, but it does not stop the still-running worker. A wedged worker could later call `runtimeContext.rewriteTranscriptEntries()` or complete/fail the task **after** the active run was cleared and a queued foreground turn proceeded, breaking the same-session wait-before-read invariant.
3. **`session.stalled` had no log backoff.** `session.stuck` and `session.long_running` already throttle repeats; `session.stalled` did not.

This change adds the bound + fence mechanism and ships it **opt-in / disabled by default**, so existing deployments whose background maintenance legitimately runs longer than a couple of minutes are not force-cancelled on upgrade. An operator hitting the wedge sets the new key to a positive millisecond value to arm it.

## User Impact

- **No behavior change on upgrade unless configured.** The per-task timeout is **disabled by default** — background turn maintenance keeps running unbounded exactly as before. There is no new force-cancel of long-running background engines on upgrade.
- Operators experiencing the wedge **opt in** by setting `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` to a positive millisecond value (absent or `0` keeps it disabled). When set, a wedged run is bounded at that value and the lane is released, so a queued user message proceeds at ~the timeout instead of waiting for the session-level abort.
- When the bound is armed and fires, late maintenance side effects are **fenced**: the runtime-owned `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper and the worker's terminal complete/fail/descriptor writes become no-ops, so a non-cooperative plugin cannot corrupt session state after the foreground turn has resumed. When the bound is disabled, the fence is never armed.
- A persistently stalled session no longer floods the logs; the first `session.stalled` warning is immediate, repeats are throttled, and recovery is never gated by the backoff.

### Changes

- `command-queue`: add an optional `onTaskTimeout` hook fired synchronously when the per-task timeout rejects, before the lane is released.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: resolve an **opt-in** per-task timeout from `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs` (absent / `0` / non-positive ⇒ no bound, no fence); when a positive value is set, pass `taskTimeoutMs` + `onTaskTimeout` to the deferred maintenance enqueue and trip a per-run fence on timeout (hook + defensive trip in the timeout catch); thread the fence into the worker and the runtime-context `rewriteTranscriptEntries` wrapper (checked at entry, inside the session-manager rewrite lock, and before the runtime-transcript write) and before the worker's `completeTaskRunByRunId` / `failTaskRunByRunId` / progress writes.
- `context-engine-maintenance`: scope the timeout classification to the resolved maintenance lane — only this deferred lane's `CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError` trips the timeout/fence path; a foreign-lane queue timeout surfacing on the enqueue falls through to the normal schedule-failure path (the lane is computed once and reused for enqueue + classification so they cannot drift).
- `session.stalled`: apply the existing `session.stuck`/`session.long_running` warn backoff (`max(last + threshold, last * 2)`), first emission immediate, recovery never gated.
- Config schema accepts `0` (`nonnegative`) as the explicit "disable" sentinel; help/types/docs document the opt-in default.
- New unit coverage: queue `onTaskTimeout` hook; timeout disabled by default and when set to `0`; configured bound + fence arming; late rewrite fenced after timeout; timed-out task not resurrected to succeeded/failed; checkpoint-after-timeout ordering; `session.stalled` backoff.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR (implemented with an AI coding agent; author reviewed and understands the change).

**Static / unit validation** (this branch):
- `tsgo:core`, `tsgo:test:src` — clean
- `command-queue.test.ts` — 34 passed; `context-engine-maintenance.test.ts` — 60 passed (incl. disabled-by-default, `0`-disables, and fence cases)
- `oxfmt --check` + oxlint on touched files — clean
- `CHANGELOG.md` not touched (left for maintainers at landing)

**Real runtime reproduction (end-to-end, in a container).** A real gateway was started in a container running this branch, with a real context-engine plugin selected via `plugins.slots.contextEngine` whose `info.turnMaintenanceMode = "background"` (so a normal `reason:"turn"` run is deferred through `scheduleDeferredTurnMaintenance`). Its `maintain()` deliberately sleeps 12s (longer than the configured timeout) and then attempts a late transcript rewrite. The bound was **explicitly opted in** for the test: `agents.defaults.compaction.turnMaintenanceTaskTimeoutMs = 5000`. Two real agent turns were run on one session. Everything in the queue/timeout/fence/transcript-rewrite path is real production code; only the plugin's deliberate sleep is contrived. Logs redacted (provider/model/host/ids replaced with placeholders):

```
[T+0.00s] [context-engine] deferred turn maintenance queued taskId=<id-1> sessionKey=<session> lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session>
[T+0.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 START                       # deferred maintenance begins, will sleep 12s
[T+2.87s] (queued) second turn is waiting behind the in-flight deferred maintenance on the session lane
[T+5.00s] [diagnostic] lane task error: lane=context-engine-turn-maintenance:<session> durationMs=5000 error="CommandLaneTaskTimeoutError: ... task timed out after 5000ms"
[T+5.00s] [agent/embedded] deferred context engine maintenance timed out: sessionKey=<session> taskId=<id-1> taskTimeoutMs=5000
[T+5.06s] [agent/embedded] embedded run start: <turn-2>   # queued turn RELEASED at the 5s timeout — NOT after the 12s wedge, NOT after the ~360s session abort
[T+12.00s] [wedge] maintain#1 WOKE after 12000ms sleep, attempting late rewrite   # the wedged worker finally wakes, 7s after the lane was released
[T+12.01s] [wedge] maintain#1 late rewrite result: {"changed":false,"bytesFreed":0,"rewrittenEntries":0,"reason":"maintenance fenced after timeout"}   # FENCED -> no-op
```

Fence scope is correct: the second turn's **foreground** maintenance (not timed out) is **not** fenced (`reason: "no replacements requested"`); only the timed-out **deferred** runs are fenced. With the bound left at its default (disabled), neither the timeout nor the fence arms and background maintenance runs unbounded as before. A scripted reproduction is available on request.

Closes #96703

AI-assisted: implemented with Codex. I reviewed the implementation, ran the repository autoreview workflow to a clean result, and verified the exact production owners against current `main`.

## What Problem This Solves

Codex and Copilot transcript mirrors decode every event in a session while holding the session writer lock just to recover idempotency facts, persisted user rows, and Codex message sequencing. A small mirror batch therefore allocates and parses in proportion to the full transcript, including on 100,000-message sessions.

## Why This Change Was Made

The transcript identity indexes now on `main` already own the required facts. This child adds a separate `withSessionTranscriptIndexedWriteLock` SDK function whose context extends the unchanged `withSessionTranscriptWriteLock` context with only three typed reads: supplied-key existence, supplied-key user messages, and the exact indexed message-event count. Codex and Copilot prepare candidate keys before acquiring the lock and query only those facts. No schema, HTTP/SSE, active-memory, cache, raw SQL surface, or generic query abstraction is added.

## User Impact

Large Codex and Copilot sessions can mirror a small batch without decoding the complete transcript under the writer lock. Dedupe identity, gateway user correlation, hooks, sequence assignment, append/update publication, and replacement behavior remain unchanged.

## Changes Walkthrough

## Summary

Implements the second [RFC #27](https://github.com/openclaw/rfcs/pull/27) slice, stacked on [#101328](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/101328):

- Creates exactly one new agent and one new workspace after a complete dry-run plan.
- Requires `--yes --plan-integrity <digest>` for mutation, rebuilds the plan in the mutating invocation, and rejects stale consent before any write.
- Rechecks agent-id and workspace ownership at the config mutation boundary.
- Preserves existing agents, defaults, bindings, models, providers, auth, and unrelated config.
- Persists pending root provenance before mutation, including source identity/integrity kind/size, manifest schema, consented plan identity, final agent/workspace, generated-config digest, owned agent path, status, and timestamps.
- Marks post-plan workspace or config races as partial and removes an empty workspace reservation when config commit fails.
- Returns versioned `openclaw.clawAddResult.v1` results with the consented plan identity.

This slice still mutates only portable agent settings and an empty workspace. Declared files, packages, MCP servers, or cron jobs fail before mutation until their canonical owner slices later in the stack. No declared component is skipped.

## Lifecycle

```text
openclaw claws add <source> --dry-run --json
# copy planIntegrity from the reviewed plan

openclaw claws add <source> --yes --plan-integrity <digest> --json
```

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where webchat users on the dark theme would see secondary text (message timestamps, slash-menu argument hints) that falls below WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1), even though the shared `--muted` token itself already meets AA on declared dark backgrounds.

## Why This Change Was Made

target.title: feat(browser): add `openclaw browser batch` CLI subcommand
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The browser runtime already supports `act:batch` (nested `actions[]` in one
`/act` call), but the CLI surface had no `batch` subcommand: a user or script
on the CLI could only run one action per `openclaw browser <action>` invocation,
so batching was reachable solely through the agent tool / HTTP route. M1.6 of
the browser tool plan closes that gap by exposing `openclaw browser batch` and
finalizing the batch semantics (ref lifecycle, target id conflicts, error
summary) in docs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Batch CLI/semantics finalization (M1.6 in the browser tool plan), scoped to
CLI exposure + docs; no runtime behavior change.

- Add `openclaw browser batch` subcommand that builds a `kind: "batch"` body
  from nested act requests and posts it to the existing `/act` route.
- `--actions <json>` for inline JSON, `--actions-file <path>` for file input,
  `--actions-file -` for stdin. `readActionsPayload` (shared.ts:151) picks the
  source; `readStdinText` (shared.ts:133) caps stdin at 1MB
  (`ACTIONS_STDIN_MAX_BYTES`, shared.ts:130) so a runaway pipe cannot fill
  memory.
- `--continue` sets `stopOnError=false`. Default omits `stopOnError` so the
  route applies its existing fail-fast default (stop on first error), matching
  the batch contract. There is no `--bail` flag because bail is the default.
- `--target-id` forwards to the batch body (same `BROWSER_TAB_REFERENCE_HELP`
  as sibling action commands).
- Outer request timeout uses `resolveBrowserActExecutionBudgetMs` so the
  batch budget covers nested actions (same path the node proxy uses for
  batch sizing).
- Docs (`docs/tools/browser-control.md` + bundled `browser-automation` skill)
  add a "Browser batch CLI" section documenting the CLI, ref lifecycle inside
  `actions[]`, `targetId` conflict handling, and the error summary format
  returned for `stopOnError=false`.

## User Impact

CLI users and scripts can now run a batch of browser actions in one call
(`openclaw browser batch --actions '[...]'` or `--actions-file -` from a
pipe), removing per-action round trips. The default fail-fast behavior is
unchanged; `--continue` is opt-in for running through all actions. No
runtime, config, or existing CLI flag changes; users who do not use the new
subcommand are unaffected.

Related: #100906

AI-assisted: yes

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where terminal users setting up a channel could not revise an earlier answer or return from the selected channel's first prompt to the channel picker. Full onboarding and `openclaw channels add` reached the same shared channel coordinator through different navigation wrappers, so Back was unavailable or stopped at the wrong boundary.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adds a typed, channel-scoped navigation outcome in the shared prompt navigator and lets the channel setup coordinator own prompt replay and rollback. Left-arrow Back revisits reversible prompts inside the selected channel; Back from that channel's first prompt returns to channel selection. Ctrl-C remains full wizard cancellation.

target.title: fix(cli): bind capability CLI media input reads to descriptor size
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `readInputFiles` helper in `src/cli/capability-cli/media-output.ts` passes user-supplied media input paths directly to `fs.readFile(path)`. While Node's implementation is usually descriptor-bound internally, the CLI has no explicit guarantee that the size validated and the bytes consumed come from the same descriptor. A concurrent writer could substitute or grow the file between the implicit stat and the read, and the function offers no graceful bound on how much data is allocated.

## Why This Change Was Made

Media input files are user-supplied paths that could be symlink-swapped or grown while the CLI is reading them. Opening the file explicitly and binding the read to the size observed on that descriptor makes the safety property visible in the code and prevents a substituted/grown file from surprising the reader, while preserving the existing unlimited-input contract.

## What Changed

Replaced `fs.readFile(path)` with an explicit descriptor-bound exact read:

```typescript
const handle = await fs.open(resolvedPath, "r");
try {
  const stat = await handle.stat();
  const size = stat.size;
  const buffer = Buffer.alloc(size);
  let offset = 0;
  while (offset < size) {
    const { bytesRead } = await handle.read(buffer, offset, size - offset, offset);
    if (bytesRead === 0) {
      throw new Error(`file shrank during read: ${resolvedPath}`);
    }
    offset += bytesRead;
  }
  return buffer;
} finally {
  await handle.close();
}
```

Key points:
- `fs.promises.open()` returns a `FileHandle`; `stat()` and the read both operate on the same descriptor.
- The read is bounded to the validated `stat.size`, so a concurrent writer cannot grow the file after the descriptor is opened.
- If the file shrinks after stat, the helper throws instead of silently returning a partial buffer, keeping failure semantics compatible with `fs.readFile`.
- The existing unlimited-input contract is preserved; no new per-file or aggregate caps are introduced.
- `try/finally` guarantees `handle.close()` even when exceptions are thrown.
- `readInputFiles` still schedules reads concurrently via `Promise.all`.

## User Impact

| Before | After |
|--------|-------|
| Input reads rely on the implicit Node `fs.readFile` contract. | Explicit descriptor-bound read makes the safety property visible and prevents post-open growth. |
| Concurrent multi-file scheduling was implicit in `fs.readFile` calls. | Explicit `Promise.all` around the new helper keeps concurrent reads. |

## Evidence

### Integration tests

All 109 capability CLI integration tests plus 3 focused media-output unit tests pass on the exact PR head:

```

Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  109 passed (109)
```

### Real CLI invocation

A real `openclaw capability image edit` invocation was run against the PR head. The input file was read through the descriptor-bound path and successfully forwarded to the image generation provider.

Command (run in a clean worktree at the PR head):

```bash
export OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR=/tmp/openclaw-proof-state
export OPENCLAW_QA_ALLOW_LOCAL_IMAGE_PROVIDER=1
openclaw capability image edit \
  --file /tmp/openclaw-proof-input.png \
  --prompt "make background transparent" \
  --model openai/gpt-image-1.5 \
  --output-format png \
  --json
```

    {

Fixes an issue where `web_fetch` could leave an upstream response body open when a non-OK (or extraction-failed) response was abandoned after a successful provider fallback return. `finally` only called `release()`; the unread (or abandoned) body was never cancelled.

## Why This Change Was Made

## User Impact

fix(markdown-core): break multi-line frontmatter value on empty lines

## Description

In `parseSimpleFrontmatterValues`, the condition `(line && !/^[ \t]/.test(line))` uses a truthy-check on `line`. An empty line (`""`) is falsy, so it bypasses the break and is incorrectly consumed as a continuation of the multi-line value. This causes blank lines between indented continuation lines to be included in the parsed value instead of terminating it.

## Fix

Removed the `line &&` guard. An empty line now correctly exits the continuation loop since `!/^[ \t]/.test("")` is `true`.

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Fal provider's `resolveFalHttpRequestConfig()` was not forwarding user-configured provider request policies (timeouts, retries, proxy settings) through `sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest`. User-configured request policies were silently ignored for Fal providers. Other providers (openrouter #104835, xai #104836) already apply this standard policy pattern.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Fal HTTP config now imports `sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest` and passes the user-configured `request` parameter to `resolveProviderHttpRequestConfig()`. All other provider logic, default request behavior, and non-HTTP transport paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

Users configuring custom request policies for Fal providers (e.g., extended timeouts for image generation) now have those settings honored instead of silently ignored.

## Evidence

- **Pattern consistency**: The `request:` parameter is now passed identically to openrouter (#104835) and xai (#104836) ??same import, same `sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest` call, same position in the config object.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check extensions/fal/http-config.ts` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- **What was NOT tested**: End-to-end integration with a real Fal API key (requires valid credentials).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Verified on PR head that `sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest` is applied to `params.req.cfg?.models?.providers?.fal?.request` before being passed to `resolveProviderHttpRequestConfig()`. The diff shows the exact same pattern as merged openrouter (#104835) and xai (#104836):

```diff
+ import { sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest } from "openclaw/plugin-sdk/provider-http";
  ...
  provider: "fal",
  capability: params.capability,
+ request: sanitizeConfiguredModelProviderRequest(
+   params.req.cfg?.models?.providers?.fal?.request,
+ ),
  transport: "http",
```

No behavioral change for users without a custom `request` config ??the sanitizer passes through `undefined` when no policy is configured.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound android-release-signing exec operations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes unbounded `execFileSync` calls in `android-release-signing.mjs` (`run()` and `runText()` helpers) that could hang indefinitely when the executed command (e.g., `jarsigner`, `zipalign`, `openssl`) is unresponsive.

## Why This Change Was Made

All `execFileSync` calls to external commands must include a timeout and kill signal. This follows the same bounding pattern applied in #109325 (docker attestation) and #110464 (verify-stable-main-closeout).

## User Impact

Android release signing steps will fail-fast within a bounded deadline instead of blocking indefinitely on hung tooling processes.

## Evidence

- Adds `ANDROID_SIGNING_TIMEOUT_MS = 120_000` constant and applies `timeout` + `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to both `run()` and `runText()` helpers.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check scripts/android-release-signing.mjs` passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Pattern consistency: matches `scripts/verify-docker-attestations.mjs` (#109325).

AI-assisted: built with Codex

---

### Real behavior proof

Probe on PR head: extracted the `run()` helper, shimmed the target command to block forever, and verified the bounded call exits with a timeout error instead of hanging.

```text
$ node proof-android-signing-timeout.mjs
entrypoint: run("sleep", ["infinity"])
fixture: command blocks forever
timeout: ANDROID_SIGNING_TIMEOUT_MS=500ms (scaled down for proof)
status: 1
stderr: Command failed: sleep infinity
        (timed out after 500ms)
```

The production deadline is 120 s; the proof scales it to 500 ms to keep the test fast. The `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` ensures the process is terminated, not just detached. Both `run()` and `runText()` helpers use the same constant and pattern.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetches the official installer and pipes it straight into bash. Current `origin/main` bounds that pipe with `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300`, but it still streams the payload directly into the shell and uses a much looser budget than the sibling e2e runner:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh (current origin/main)
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 -- "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

This PR brings the non-root runner to the same **download-then-execute** contract as the sibling e2e runner merged in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`): download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, verify curl completed, then execute it, then clean up.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fail fast on stall:** `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged for the sibling installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911). A stalled fetch fails the step in under 2 minutes instead of tying up the runner for 5.
- **No partial-stream execution:** with the temp-file form, bash only ever runs a fully downloaded installer; curl's exit status gates execution (`set -euo pipefail`).
- **Consistency:** both Docker install-sh lanes now share the same fetch contract.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download fails fast with a clear curl error instead of streaming into a long-hanging pipe. Identical install semantics on success.

## Evidence

After (this PR, `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh`):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
# Download the installer to a temp file first so a stalled connection or hung
# response body cannot wedge the container run forever. Piping curl straight to
# bash inherits curl's default of no total timeout.
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Regression tests (final head `15ad709b`, rebased onto latest main):

```bash
pnpm vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  77 passed (77)
```

Coverage includes a controlled stalled-transfer probe: the bounded fetch aborts on stall (the exact failure mode this change defends against), and the temp installer file is cleaned up via the EXIT trap. The runner-assertion test now checks the bounded temp-file form (`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer"` + `bash "$installer"`).

## Real Docker smoke (current head `d1a1adef6e0`, rebased onto latest main)

Full non-root Docker smoke against the real installer endpoint (`https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`), colima/arm64, image built from `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/Dockerfile` (which COPYs this head's `run.sh`), exact harness env (`OPENCLAW_NO_ONBOARD=1`, `OPENCLAW_NO_PROMPT=1`, `OPENCLAW_INSTALL_METHOD=npm`):

```text
==> Pre-flight: ensure git absent
==> Pre-flight: ensure supported Node is already present
==> Run installer (non-root user)          # download-to-file + bash "$installer" path under test
✓ Git installed
✓ npm configured for user installs
✓ OpenClaw npm package installed
✓ OpenClaw installed
🦞 OpenClaw installed successfully (2026.7.1-2)!
==> Verify git installed
==> Verify CLI installed
cli=openclaw installed=2026.7.1-2 expected=2026.7.1-2
==> Sanity: CLI runs
OK
```

The download-then-execute success path works end-to-end in the real non-root container: the bounded curl fetch completes to a temp file, `bash "$installer"` runs it, git and the CLI verify, and the runner exits `OK`.

## What was not tested

Nothing material: the success path is proven by the real Docker run above, the stall path by the hermetic stalled-transfer probe in the suite.

## CI note

The previous head failed `checks-node-compact-small-1` because the branch's own runner assertion still expected the old piped form (`curl ... | bash`) that this PR replaces. The assertion is aligned with the temp-file fetch on the current head, and the branch is rebased onto latest main.

- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance

- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

## Summary

In this PR, the Appearance text-size setting applies across Control UI content typography instead of only affecting the chat transcript. Shared content font sizes now route through `--control-ui-text-scale`, while touch-primary text-entry controls keep the existing 16px minimum so the 90% text-size stop does not reintroduce mobile Safari focus zoom.

## Screenshots

Settings at the default M text size, showing the Appearance text-size control in English.

![Settings text size at M](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-settings-text-size-m-en.png)

Overview at XXL text size, showing the larger page typography across cards and form controls.

![Overview using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-overview-xxl-en.png)

![Channels using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-channels-xxl-en.png)

Mobile Overview at XXL text size, showing the narrow layout with scaled content typography.

![Mobile overview using XXL text size](https://mystic-bonnet-p3d4.here.now/pr-100934-mobile-overview-xxl-en.png)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes the Appearance text-size setting so it affects Control UI content typography beyond the chat transcript. Before this PR, the setting could be saved while many Settings, quick settings, overview, channel, session, skill, and content surfaces still used fixed font sizes.

## Why This Change Was Made

In this PR, shared Control UI font sizes route through the existing `--control-ui-text-scale` value instead of hard-coded pixel sizes. The change keeps layout chrome and spacing stable while letting readable content, forms, cards, chat text, composer text, and page typography respond to S/M/L/XL/XXL.

Touch-primary text-entry controls keep the existing `--control-ui-input-text-size` minimum so the 90% text-size stop does not shrink mobile inputs below 16px and reintroduce Safari focus zoom.

## User Impact

Changing Text size in Appearance now produces visible typography changes across the main product surfaces, while M remains the normal/default size.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

target.body:
## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`
